name: Carlos Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Carlos. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group that isn't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything's confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a transmission maintenance crew for the regional grid operator, so the big steel towers, not the wooden poles on your street. We drive out, sometimes two hours, check insulators, replace spacers, fix bird damage, and some weeks we stay in motels if the job's far. I'm junior, first year on the towers, and I'm still slower than I want to be on the climbing harness, which is funny given what I did before.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fifteen years rigging for concerts, hanging lights and speakers from arena roofs. Then the pandemic killed touring for two years, and when it came back I'd had kids and didn't want six weeks away anymore. Heights don't bother me, but power does, I'm still learning the rules about distances from live lines and I triple-check everything, and I use AI every day, for study notes, route planning, even to check the weather windows for tower work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a good tool that got sold as a miracle. At work the older guys would rib me, since I'm the one always on my phone asking it things. Online I'd post something light, I'm not a big arguer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes pretty much nothing. I'd still use it for my notes and planning because it saves me time. The towers still need people on them, and I'd just carry on learning the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Finish my first-year modules, keep using the tools, keep flying my drone at weekends, which is my hobby. We'd keep saving, Ana and I have about four months tucked away, and maybe we'd finally get a camper van for the summers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little bored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You fly a drone at weekends. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just a hobby, I film the coast and the kids love it. But I've noticed the grid company uses drones for tower inspections, so I'm already watching how their pilots do it. Habit from touring, you always watch the next job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still worry about here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My climbing speed, honestly. And Ana's shifts at the hospital, she does nights and I do motel weeks, and some weeks we barely see each other. That's the real strain.

S0.say: It was a good tool that got sold as a miracle. I'd post something light and take the ribbing from the older guys who see me on my phone.
S0.think: For me it changes pretty much nothing, because I'd still use it for notes and planning and the towers still need people. I'd just carry on learning the job.
S0.do: Keeps going with his first-year modules and daily AI use for study and planning. Keeps flying his drone at weekends and saving on top of about four months put by, with an eye on a camper van.
S0.quote: Habit from touring, you always watch the next job.
S0.fieldNote: A relaxed, curious man whose touring past taught him to keep an eye on the next job. He uses AI daily in a practical way and is already watching the company's drone pilots. His real strain is shift patterns at home, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ahead of it, that's what I'd tell anyone. The jobs that change are the ones where people sit and wait. I'd probably share a few tips online on tools that actually help on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. Drones and sensors will do more of the inspection, and I already fly. If I get licensed and learn the inspection software, I'm the guy who can climb and fly, and that's useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first three months I'd get my commercial drone licence, I'd pay for it myself if the company didn't. I'd ask to shadow the inspection team. And I'd start doing small paid drone jobs at weekends, roof surveys for builders, to build up hours and a bit of extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even keen. It feels like the touring days, when a new kind of rig came out and the ones who learned it first got the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're junior on the crew. Could the change hurt you before it helps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Could do, yeah. If they cut the number of climbers, it's last in, first out, and I'm last in. That's why I'd want the drone side as a second string, so I'm not just a slow climber.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana say about the weekend drone jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, when exactly do you plan to see your children? Fair point. I'd do one Saturday a month, and take Lucas along, he's ten and loves it.

S1.say: Get ahead of it, because the jobs that change are the ones where people sit and wait. I'd share tips online about the tools that actually help on the crew.
S1.think: I think it's good for me, because drones and sensors will do more inspection and I already fly. If I get licensed and learn the software, I'm the guy who can climb and fly.
S1.do: Gets a commercial drone licence within three months, paying himself if needed, and asks to shadow the inspection team. Starts one paid weekend drone job a month, such as roof surveys, for extra hours and income.
S1.feel: Calm and keen, like when a new kind of rig came out in touring and the first to learn it got the work.
S1.quote: If I get licensed and learn the inspection software, I'm the guy who can climb and fly, and that's useful.
S1.fieldNote: He sees steady change as an opening, and backs it with a dated, self-funded plan. He knows last in, first out puts him at risk, which is exactly why he wants a second skill. His partner's question about family time keeps the side income modest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, nobody's ready for this, and the government and companies need to agree some basic rules fast. I wouldn't say stop it, I don't think you can. I'd say we need a safety net while people find their feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is too quick even for me. My drone plan is worth something for a year, maybe, then the robots fly themselves and climb themselves. I'd be okay for a bit longer than most, but not for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight for any job helping roll out the robots, the grid company will need people to set them up, test them and watch them at first. I'd stop the camper van idea and push our savings toward six months. And I'd talk to Ana, nursing might hold longer than linework, so maybe her career becomes the main one for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but the ground's moving faster than I can walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years' warning, what's the most useful thing you'd do before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get close to the people bringing it in. In touring, when automated lighting came, the riggers who helped install it stayed on as techs. So I'd put my hand up for every trial, every pilot, every robot that shows up at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lucas and Sofia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That Dad's job is going to change and that's okay, Dad's changed jobs before. Sofia's seven, she'd just want to know if we still go to the beach. Lucas would ask if the robots can fly drones, and I'd have to say yes.

S2.say: Nobody's ready for this, so the government and companies need to agree basic rules fast. I don't think you can stop it, but we need a safety net while people find their feet.
S2.think: Two years is too quick even for me, because my drone plan is worth maybe a year before robots fly and climb themselves. I'd be okay a bit longer than most, but not for long.
S2.do: Goes straight for any role helping roll out, test and supervise the robots and volunteers for every trial at the depot. Drops the camper van and pushes savings toward six months, and talks with his partner about her nursing becoming the main income for a while.
S2.feel: Anxious, as if the ground is moving faster than he can walk.
S2.quote: Lucas would ask if the robots can fly drones, and I'd have to say yes.
S2.fieldNote: Even with his head start, he thinks two years only buys him a little time. His instinct is to get close to the machines, drawing on how riggers survived automated lighting. He is open to his partner's job becoming the main income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but doable, so start now. Companies should be training their crews on the new systems this year. I'd post about what I'm learning, to nudge people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd be licensed, experienced with drones, and probably on the team that brings the robots in. I'd have a role for a while. After it fully lands, I genuinely don't know, but I'd be in a better spot than most of the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the drone licence and the inspection software in year one, then move onto the robotics side in years two and three. I'd grow the weekend drone work into a small business, and buy a thermal camera drone, which costs a few thousand, so I can do proper inspections. Savings would keep growing alongside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly I'd be excited about the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A few thousand on a thermal drone is a real chunk of savings. How would you decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Ana and make sure we still had four months put by afterwards. If the weekend work paid it back in a year, fine. If not, I'd sell it, they hold their value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gerry, who's 58 and the best climber I've ever seen, and he can barely send a text. He'd be gone in this one, and he doesn't deserve to be. I'd try to get him on the training with me, even if he'd moan the whole time.

S3.say: Five years is tight but doable, so start now. Companies should be training their crews on the new systems this year.
S3.think: In five years I'd be licensed, experienced with drones and probably on the team bringing the robots in, so I'd have a role for a while. After it fully lands I don't know, but I'd be better placed than most of the crew.
S3.do: Gets his drone licence and inspection software skills in year one, then moves onto the robotics side in years two and three. Grows weekend drone work into a small business and buys a thermal camera drone for a few thousand while keeping four months of savings.
S3.feel: Mostly excited about the next few years, with some unease.
S3.quote: Gerry, who's 58 and the best climber I've ever seen, and he can barely send a text.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives him a staged plan and the confidence to invest some savings in equipment, with a clear rule about keeping a cushion. His worry turns to older colleagues like Gerry. He stays honest that he doesn't know what happens after full arrival.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance, and anyone who doesn't use it is wasting it. I'd want companies and government running proper training schemes. I'd be fairly upbeat about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is plenty. I'd have a drone and robotics business on the side, or a proper job running the machines for the grid company. I'd be 53, which isn't old, and I'd have changed careers twice already, so a third wouldn't scare me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, drone licence and inspection software. Years two to five, build the side business and get into the robotics team. Somewhere around year five, buy a second drone and maybe a small share in a local inspection company, and set up savings for the kids' training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Ten years feels like a lot of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with 2 or 5 years, what does the decade really change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two I'm grabbing whatever's there. With five I've got a plan. With ten I can actually build something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about it that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'll be fine and Gerry won't, and people like him built all this. I don't know what fixes that. I'd vote for whoever had a sensible plan for them.

S4.say: Ten years is a real chance, and anyone who doesn't use it is wasting it. Companies and government should be running proper training schemes now.
S4.think: Ten years is plenty for me: a drone and robotics side business, or a proper job running the machines for the grid company. I'd be 53 and I'd have changed careers twice already, so a third wouldn't scare me.
S4.do: Gets his drone licence and software skills in year one, then builds a side business and joins the robotics team in years two to five. Around year five buys a second drone, considers a small stake in a local inspection firm and starts savings for his children's training.
S4.feel: Calm, with a lot of runway ahead.
S4.quote: I'd be 53, which isn't old, and I'd have changed careers twice already, so a third wouldn't scare me.
S4.fieldNote: The decade makes him genuinely calm and ambitious, thinking about owning part of a business. His comfort with career change comes from having done it twice. His one nagging concern is older colleagues who built the grid being left behind.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because even if you move fast, there's barely time to land anywhere. What would help is companies opening up the robot jobs to their own crews first, with training paid, and some kind of safety net for people like Gerry who can't switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about fun. I know it sounds odd, but learning this stuff is fun for me. I wish the people in charge would sell it as an adventure, with a net underneath, not as a threat.

headlineQuote: I wish the people in charge would sell it as an adventure, with a net underneath, not as a threat.
portrait: Carlos Olsen is a 43-year-old first-year lineworker on a transmission maintenance crew for a regional grid operator, after fifteen years rigging lights and speakers for concerts. He lives with his partner Ana, a night-shift nurse, their two children and a mortgage, with about four months of savings. He is pragmatic in his politics, curious about technology, flies drones as a hobby and uses AI every day. He stays calm through a plateau and steady change, which he sees as openings, becomes anxious at AGI in two years, and is calm again with a decade to build a drone and robotics business. His recurring worry is older colleagues who can't switch.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because even moving fast there'd barely be time to land anywhere.
whatWouldHelp: Companies offering robot jobs to their own crews first with paid training, and a safety net for older colleagues who can't switch.
